reviews.reasoning: Span Ps.64.1-Ps.64.6 and its rear seam hold on re-derivation. The opening warrant is tier-1 text: the counted superscription (web:Ps.64.0 = oshb:Ps.64.1) לַמְנַצֵּ֗חַ מִזְמ֥וֹר לְדָוִֽד, then the imperative petition opening the body, (web:Ps.64.1 = oshb:Ps.64.2) שְׁמַע אֱלֹהִ֣ים קוֹלִ֣י בְשִׂיחִ֑י, then the relative chain the row cites, which I re-collated at byte tier at oshb:Ps.64.4 (= web:Ps.64.3). The rear seam at web:Ps.64.6|web:Ps.64.7 (= oshb:Ps.64.7|oshb:Ps.64.8) is carried by the wayyiqtol subject reversal to God at oshb:Ps.64.8, which I collated at byte tier, and both witnesses agree on the pivot; of the 2 adjacent candidate seams 1 verse either side, 0 of 2 carry a better tier-1 warrant. 4 of 4 pointed quotes in the row collate at byte tier. pmarks_Ps.json records 0 selah verses, 0 ketiv/qere notes and 0 reversed-nun segs in Ps 64, so no disclosure is owed and the row asserts no such mark. Two defects stand: the rationale's title dual-cite is arithmetically wrong, and the third-person-plural continuity signal is falsified at the closing verse of the span itself. The rationale also names the relative particle in unpointed consonantal form; that is a lexeme mention rather than a quotation, and it is followed at once by the byte-true pointed form at oshb:Ps.64.4 with its ref, so I do not treat it as a quotation defect.

challenges.claim: The rationale equates the WEB title pseudo-ref with MT 64:2, but the counted superscription of Ps 64 is MT 64:1; the row's own boundary_evidence_refs carry the correct pairing, so the field contradicts the refs and uses oshb:Ps.64.2 for 2 different verses.
challenges.evidence: web_mt_offset_map.json gives Ps 64 rule=shift k=1 with mt_title_verses [1], and ps_lib.web_to_mt(64, 0) returns (64, 1); psalm_device_inventory.json superscriptions['64'] likewise records mt_title_verses [1]. The counted superscription is (web:Ps.64.0 = oshb:Ps.64.1) לַמְנַצֵּ֗חַ מִזְמ֥וֹר לְדָוִֽד, collated byte tier, rendered “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David.” (web:Ps.64.0). MT 64:2 is not the title but the opening body verse, (web:Ps.64.1 = oshb:Ps.64.2) שְׁמַע אֱלֹהִ֣ים קוֹלִ֣י בְשִׂיחִ֑י, collated byte tier, rendered “Hear my voice, God, in my complaint.” (web:Ps.64.1) — and the same rationale cites (oshb:Ps.64.2) for exactly that quote one clause later, so the field asserts oshb:Ps.64.2 is both the title and the body opening. The row's boundary_evidence_refs entry reads 'web:Ps.64.0 = oshb:Ps.64.1', which is correct and contradicts the rationale. This survived the gate because citation_sweep.py runs its dual-cite arithmetic arm over boundary_evidence_refs entries and not over prose; in-prose dual pairs reach a warn-only arm, so the sweep reported status GREEN with 0 problems on this cluster. The same wrong formula appears in M8-Ps-179 for Ps 65, so the cure is one authored edit installed on both title-bearing rows in the same pass.

challenges.claim: The signal that third-person plural verbs run continuously from oshb:Ps.64.4 through the end of this span is falsified at the span's closing verse, which carries a first-person-plural qatal and ends in a verbless clause with a singular subject.
challenges.evidence: The closing verse of the span is (web:Ps.64.6 = oshb:Ps.64.7) יַֽחְפְּֽשׂוּ עוֹלֹ֗ת תַּ֭מְנוּ חֵ֣פֶשׂ מְחֻפָּ֑שׂ וְקֶ֥רֶב אִ֝֗ישׁ וְלֵ֣ב עָמֹֽק, collated byte tier against oshb:Ps.64.7. Its third word-group is the pointed form תַּ֭מְנוּ, a 1st-person-common-plural qatal (the 3mp qatal of this root is written without the nun); a skeleton sweep of that spelling returns 1 verse book-wide, MT Ps.64.7 = web:Ps.64.6. Both witnesses read it as 1st person plural: WEB renders the clause as direct speech, “We have made a perfect plan!” (web:Ps.64.6), and a WEB phrase sweep of that wording returns 1 verse book-wide. The same verse then closes with וְקֶ֥רֶב אִ֝֗ישׁ וְלֵ֣ב עָמֹֽק — a verbless clause whose subject is singular — rendered “Surely man’s mind and heart are cunning.” (web:Ps.64.6). The staged extract has 0 morphology fields, so the form is argued from the pointed bytes plus both witnesses' renderings, which agree here. The span itself is unaffected; the defect is the substrate signal offered for it.

reviews.reasoning: Span Ps.64.7-Ps.64.10 verifies on the arms I can test. The opening warrant is the wayyiqtol subject reversal to God at (web:Ps.64.7 = oshb:Ps.64.8), which I collated at byte tier from the source bytes; the row's rear boundary is the psalm's own end (WEB 64 has 10 verses, MT 64 has 11), so no seam rival exists there. 2 of 2 Hebrew runs collate at byte tier and 4 of 4 English quotes are verbatim WEB at their cited refs. 4 of 4 boundary_evidence_refs entries carry correct dual-cite arithmetic under the +1 rule for Ps 64. I re-derived both counts the row leans on rather than trusting them: psalm_device_inventory.json yhwh_elohim_per_psalm['64'] is {"yhwh": 1, "elohim": 3}, and summing that field over Ps 60-65 gives yhwh 1 and elohim 22 — both figures the row states, exact, with the token object named as the inventory defines it. The 1 Yahweh token is (web:Ps.64.10 = oshb:Ps.64.11) בַּ֭יהוָה, an inseparable-prefixed unsuffixed noun form, which sits inside the inventory's counting object. pmarks_Ps.json records 0 selah verses, 0 ketiv/qere notes and 0 reversed-nun segs in Ps 64, so the row owes no disclosure and asserts no such mark. Confidence high is calibrated. Observation, not a challenge: the rationale and the second substrate signal both say 'this part's', a reference to the authoring partition rather than to the text; unlike the decision-id in M8-Ps-179 the phrase is self-glossed in the same breath by 'Ps 60-65 together carry 1 yhwh against 22 elohim', so the scope stays verse-anchored and recoverable by a reader of the finished chunk, and I do not contest it.

The span Ps.65.1-Ps.65.4 and its rear seam survive re-derivation: the unit runs from the body opening (web:Ps.65.1 = oshb:Ps.65.2) to the temple beatitude at (web:Ps.65.4 = oshb:Ps.65.5), and the turn to cosmic answer at (web:Ps.65.5 = oshb:Ps.65.6) is a real register shift, so the seam is the better of the 2 candidates the row weighs. 2 of 2 Hebrew runs collate at byte tier and 4 of 4 English quotes carrying a web: ref are verbatim WEB. pmarks_Ps.json records 0 selah verses, 0 ketiv/qere notes and 0 reversed-nun segs in Ps 65; the 7 paseq segs recorded at MT Ps.65.5, 65.6, 65.8, 65.9, 65.10 and 65.14 are seg-layer and uncited here, so nothing is owed. The row's root observation is sound and says 'root' rather than 'spelling': the plene spelling behind the Ps 62 pair returns 4 verses book-wide by skeleton sweep, 2 of them in Ps 62 (Ps.62.2, Ps.62.6), while the Ps 65 form is written defectively and returns 1 verse book-wide, so the shared item is the root and not the string. Four defects stand, one of them the same wrong title arithmetic as M8-Ps-177. A further imprecision I note without filing: the substrate signal says the quoted words 'open the psalm' when they open the body, the psalm opening with the counted superscription.

The row's boundary_evidence_refs entry 'web:Ps.65.0 = oshb:Ps.65.1' is correct and contradicts the rationale. citation_sweep.py returns GREEN because its dual-cite arithmetic arm reads boundary_evidence_refs and not prose.

The reference is recoverable without the id: a skeleton sweep of the plene spelling returns 4 verses book-wide (Ps.22.3, Ps.39.3, Ps.62.2, Ps.62.6), of which the 2 in Ps 62 are MT Ps.62.2 = web:Ps.62.1 and MT Ps.62.6 = web:Ps.62.5, so a verse-anchored formulation carrying the same content is available at no evidential cost.

reviews.reasoning: The span Ps.65.5-Ps.65.8 is right and I do not contest it: the front seam at (web:Ps.65.5 = oshb:Ps.65.6) is a genuine register turn, and the rear seam before the harvest material at (web:Ps.65.9 = oshb:Ps.65.10) is the better of the 2 candidates. The row's central evidence re-derives cleanly: the 2 verse-initial participles it names, at (web:Ps.65.6 = oshb:Ps.65.7) and (web:Ps.65.7 = oshb:Ps.65.8), collate at byte tier 2 of 2, sit verse-initial in the source bytes 2 of 2, read as mem-preformative hiphil participles on the pointing, and the signal names its unit and carries its digit ('2 verses'). 3 of 3 Hebrew runs collate at byte tier and 4 of 4 English quotes are verbatim WEB at their refs; 4 of 4 boundary_evidence_refs entries carry correct dual-cite arithmetic under the +1 rule. pmarks_Ps.json records 0 selah verses and 0 ketiv/qere notes in Ps 65, and the paseq recorded at MT Ps.65.6 is seg-layer and outside the quotable bytes, so the row's byte-contiguous quote across that position is legitimate and owes no disclosure. What I contest is the close-warrant's description of the rear-seam verse and a missing mirrored ref.

challenges.claim: The row describes its closing verse as the distant peoples' awe and quotes 1 of its 2 sentences, omitting that the verse's second colon returns to second-person divine address — the same address that opens the next span, so a device straddles this row's rear seam undisclosed.
challenges.evidence: The closing verse of the span is (web:Ps.65.8 = oshb:Ps.65.9) וַיִּ֤ירְא֨וּ יֹשְׁבֵ֣י קְ֭צָוֺת מֵאוֹתֹתֶ֑יךָ מ֤וֹצָֽאֵי בֹ֖קֶר וָעֶ֣רֶב תַּרְנִֽין, collated byte tier against oshb:Ps.65.9. Its opening colon already carries a second-person-masculine-singular suffix in מֵאוֹתֹתֶ֑יךָ, and its second colon closes on תַּרְנִֽין, which WEB reads as address to God: “You call the morning’s dawn and the evening with songs of joy.” (web:Ps.65.8). The row's rationale quotes “They also who dwell in faraway places are afraid at your wonders” (web:Ps.65.8) and glosses the close as 'the distant peoples’ awe', and its rejected_alternative repeats that reading; 0 of the row's fields disclose the second colon. That matters at this seam because the next span opens on the same second-person address, (web:Ps.65.9 = oshb:Ps.65.10) פָּקַ֥דְתָּ, a 2ms qatal — byte-true second-person address therefore runs across the row's own rear seam. The campaign rule is that a device straddling a row's seam argues continuity against the row unless disclosed. I am not proposing a different seam: the topical break before the harvest material still carries it, but the close-warrant as written misdescribes half the verse it rests on.

reviews.reasoning: The span Ps.65.9-Ps.65.13 is correct: it opens on the tense and topic pivot at (web:Ps.65.9 = oshb:Ps.65.10) and closes the psalm, so its rear boundary is the psalm's own end and cannot be contested. 2 of 2 Hebrew runs collate at byte tier, both form claims re-derive from the pointed bytes — the opening form is a 2ms qatal and the psalm's closing verse does open with a 3rd-person plural qatal on nature as subject, and both witnesses agree — and 2 of 2 English quotes are verbatim WEB at their refs. 5 of 5 boundary_evidence_refs entries carry correct dual-cite arithmetic, including the psalm-final pair (web:Ps.65.13 = oshb:Ps.65.14). pmarks_Ps.json records 0 selah verses, 0 ketiv/qere notes and 0 reversed-nun segs in the span. The rejected_alternative is a fair one-sentence rival and I agree with its resolution: 0 tier-1 signals mark web:Ps.65.12 as a fresh strophe. I also checked the substantive claim about the Davidic run and it is true, so the defect that remains is that the row credits a governance file for it in row prose. A minor imprecision I note without filing: 'the furrows and showers (web:Ps.65.10-web:Ps.65.11)' attributes to a 2-verse range an image that sits in web:Ps.65.10 alone, web:Ps.65.11 being the year's crown and the overflowing carts.

challenges.claim: The rationale cites the book strategy inside row prose as the authority for the Davidic run, which the register rule bans outright, though the claim is independently true from the device inventory.

The standing register rule admits 0 strategy-file citations in row prose. The attribution is also unnecessary: psalm_device_inventory.json superscriptions carries the le_david label on 15 of the 15 consecutive psalms Ps 51 through Ps 65, and superscriptions['66'] carries labels mizmor, shir, lamnatseach with 0 le_david, which is the break that ends the run; five_books puts Book II at Ps 42-72. A source-anchored formulation therefore carries the same content, and the replacement warrant passes the test that killed the original in the same edit.
